summary: Updates the ASN.1 modules for the PKIX certificate format and related formats from the 1988 to the 2002 version of ASN.1. Nothing changes on the wire; only the syntax used to describe them is brought up to date. It is informational.

eli5.summary: The way certificates are described gets a modern rewrite. The certificates themselves look exactly the same.

questions: what changed from 1988 asn.1 to 2002 asn.1
subtitle: The PKIX certificate formats rewritten in the 2002 version of ASN.1, with identical bits on the wire.

tldr.problem: Most security RFCs, including those for PKIX, CMS and S/MIME, still used ASN.1 from the 1988 standard, which has been deprecated.
tldr.mechanism: The document republishes the ASN.1 modules for a set of PKIX RFCs in the 2002 syntax, using its object model in place of the old ANY holes, plus two shared modules of common definitions.
tldr.outcome: Nothing changes on the wire. The document is Informational, and has been updated by RFC 6960, RFC 9480 and RFC 9810.

today: RFC 5912 is an Informational RFC that has been updated by RFC 6960, RFC 9480 and RFC 9810. Its companion for CMS and S/MIME is RFC 5911.

sections.title: Why New ASN.1 Modules
sections.content:
ASN.1 is the notation the PKIX certificate format and many related formats are written in. Some developers wanted the IETF to use the latest version of it, but most security RFCs still used the 1988 version, which has been deprecated. That is particularly true of the standards for PKIX, Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) and S/MIME.

This document brings the PKIX modules up to the 2002 version of ASN.1. It states plainly that there are no bits-on-the-wire changes to any of the formats; it is only a change to the syntax.
sections.eli5: It is like rewriting a recipe in clearer modern language. The food that comes out is exactly the same.

sections.title: Which RFCs Are Covered
sections.content:
The document supplies updated modules for the following RFCs, in this order: RFC 2560 (OCSP), RFC 2986 (PKCS #10 certificate requests), RFC 3279 (PKIX algorithms and identifiers), RFC 3852 (attribute certificates, version 1), RFC 4055 (additional RSA algorithms), RFC 4210 (CMP), RFC 4211 (CRMF), RFC 5055 (SCVP), RFC 5272 (CMC), RFC 5280 (the certificate and CRL profile, both explicit and implicit modules) and RFC 5755 (attribute certificates, version 2).

Not every module is actually updated; some are included only to make the set complete. The companion RFC 5911 does the same for CMS and S/MIME.
sections.eli5: It is a big binder with the rewritten pages for lots of different certificate-related rulebooks, all in one place.

sections.title: The Object Model and Naming Prefixes
sections.content:
The modules lean heavily on the object model available in the 2002 ASN.1 documents. Objects are defined for each kind of algorithm, and every place where the 1988 syntax had an ANY hole for variable syntax now uses objects instead.

To make names easy to scan, the document adopts short prefixes that show what kind of object a name refers to. For example, id-sha1 is the object identifier while mda-sha1 is the message digest object for sha1. Each module defines object sets with one consistent name per algorithm type, such as PublicKeys. When two modules use the same set name, an importing module tells them apart with the module name, as in PKIXAlgs-2008.PublicKeys.
sections.eli5: Every kind of thing gets a short tag on its name, like labelling boxes "toys" and "books", so you can tell what is inside without opening it.

sections.title: Shared Modules and Self-Contained Sets
sections.content:
Two modules do not come from any existing RFC: PKIX-CommonTypes and AlgorithmInformation. They hold common definitions used throughout this document and in RFC 5911. The common types include the ATTRIBUTE and EXTENSION classes, AttributeSet, SingleAttribute and Extensions. The algorithm module defines classes for digest, signature, key transport, key agreement, key wrap, key derivation, MAC, public key and content encryption algorithms.

Some modules take definitions from different places than the original RFCs did. The aim is that these modules, combined with those in RFC 5911, stand on their own without importing from anywhere else. The comments inside the modules still point to the original RFCs, and some of those references may since have been superseded by later RFCs.
sections.eli5: Two of the chapters are brand-new shared toolboxes. All the other chapters borrow tools from them instead of looking all over the house.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Even though all the RFCs covered are security-related, the document itself has no security considerations. The ASN.1 modules keep the same bits on the wire as the modules they replace.
sections.eli5: Because the certificates look exactly the same as before, nothing new needs guarding.
